How does Terraform communicate with clou: Terraform core talks to a provider plugin (a separate binary, e.g. the Google or AWS provider) over gRPC using a well-defined plugin protocol - the provider translates Terraform's generic resource CRUD operations into actual cloud API calls (REST/SDK calls to GCP/AWS), and translates responses back into Terraform's internal resource state representation. This plugin architecture is why adding support for a new cloud is 'just' writing a new provider rather than modifying Terraform core itself.
What is the purpose of a provider in Ter: A provider is the plugin that implements the actual integration with a specific API (GCP, AWS, Kubernetes, Datadog, etc.) - it defines the resource and data source types available for that platform, handles authentication, and translates Terraform's plan/apply operations into real API calls. Without a provider block configured, Terraform has no way to know how to create, read, update, or delete any resource for that platform.
What is the difference between a resourc: A `resource` block tells Terraform to create and manage a real object (Terraform owns its lifecycle - create, update, destroy). A `data` source is read-only - it looks up information about an existing object (one Terraform doesn't manage, or one created elsewhere in the same config) and exposes it for reference elsewhere in your configuration, without ever creating, modifying, or destroying that object.
What are input variables, local values,: Input variables (`variable` blocks) parameterize a module/configuration from the outside, letting the same code be reused with different values. Local values (`locals`) are internal computed values used to avoid repeating an expression multiple times within the same configuration - they're not settable from outside. Output values (`output` blocks) expose specific values from a module/configuration for use by the caller (a parent module, a `terraform_remote_state` data source, or CI/CD tooling).
What are the data types supported in Ter: Primitive types: string, number, bool. Collection types: list (ordered sequence), set (unordered, unique values), map (key-value pairs). Structural types: object (fixed set of named attributes with specific types) and tuple (fixed-length sequence with specific types per position). Variables can be typed explicitly with `type = ...` to get validation errors early rather than a confusing failure deep in a resource block.
Can a list be passed as an input variabl: Yes - declare `variable "names" { type = list(string) }` and pass a list value either via a `.tfvars` file, `-var` CLI flag (with HCL list syntax), or an environment variable with JSON-encoded value; within the configuration, iterate over it with `for_each` or `count`, or index into it directly (`var.names[0]`).
Can a map be passed as an input variable: Yes - declare `variable "tags" { type = map(string) }` and pass key-value pairs; maps are commonly used with `for_each` (iterating over `var.tags` gives you both the key and value per iteration) or for structured configuration like per-environment settings keyed by environment name.
Can a for expression iterate over a list: Yes - `[for item in var.list : upper(item)]` produces a new list by transforming each element, and `[for item in var.list : item if item != ""]` adds filtering. The same `for` expression syntax works over maps and sets too, with `for k, v in var.map : ...` giving access to both key and value.
Explain the following expression:\nfor_e: This is a `for` expression building a map from a list: it iterates over `var.records` (a list of objects, each presumably with `name` and `type` fields) and produces a map where each key is a computed unique string (`name-type`) and each value is the full original record object. This map is then fed directly into `for_each` so Terraform creates one resource instance per record, using that computed string as the resource instance's stable key.
What is the purpose of:\n\"${record.name: This constructs the map's key-value pair for one iteration: the key (left of `=>`) is a unique string built from the record's name and type, and the value (right of `=>`) is the entire record object, preserved so it's accessible as `each.value` inside the resource block that uses this `for_each`.
Why do we concatenate the record name an: Because `for_each` requires a map with unique keys, and a DNS record is only uniquely identified by the combination of name AND type (e.g. the same name can have both an A record and a TXT record) - using just the name alone as the key would collide if two records share a name but differ in type, causing Terraform to error or silently drop one of them.
How does Terraform store each resource's: Every resource instance is stored in the state file as a JSON object containing its resource address, provider-reported attributes (the full set of fields returned by the API after creation, not just what you specified), dependencies, and metadata like the provider version used - this is what lets `terraform plan` compute an accurate diff against real infrastructure on every run without re-querying every attribute from the API each time.
How are resources stored in the Terrafor: Each instance is stored keyed by its `for_each` key rather than a numeric index - the resource address looks like `google_dns_record_set.record["www-A"]` instead of `[0]`. This is the key advantage of `for_each` over `count`: removing or reordering an item from the middle of the source map only affects that specific keyed instance, rather than shifting every subsequent numeric index and causing Terraform to plan to destroy/recreate unrelated resources.
Can you explain the alias block (or SOA: In Terraform provider context, an `alias` on a `provider` block lets you configure multiple instances of the same provider (e.g. two AWS regions) and reference a specific one per resource via `provider = aws.us_west`. In DNS context, an SOA (Start of Authority) record holds administrative information about a zone - the primary nameserver, admin contact, and refresh/retry/expire/TTL timers used by secondary nameservers for zone transfers.
What is the purpose of terraform import?: `terraform import` brings an already-existing real-world resource (created outside Terraform, e.g. via console or another tool) under Terraform's management by writing its current state into the state file, matched against a resource block you've already written in configuration - it does not generate the configuration itself (in older Terraform versions), only the state entry, so the `.tf` code must already describe that resource correctly or the next plan will show a large diff.
During code restructuring, why don't we: Because the resource already exists in state - restructuring (e.g. moving a resource into a module, or renaming it) is a state-addressing change, not a 'this resource is new to Terraform' situation, so the correct tool is `terraform state mv` (or the `moved` block in newer Terraform versions), which relocates the existing state entry to its new address without touching the real infrastructure at all. Using `import` here would be redundant at best and risks creating a duplicate/orphaned state entry at worst.
How do you modularize Terraform code wit: Use `terraform state mv` (or a `moved` block) to relocate each resource's state address to its new location inside the module, matching the new module's resource addresses exactly, then run `terraform plan` to confirm zero changes are proposed - a clean plan (no add/destroy) confirms the refactor only changed where resources live in your codebase, not the real infrastructure.
What precautions do you take while modul: Always run `terraform plan` after each state move and before considering the refactor done - a plan showing unexpected creates/destroys means an address mapping was wrong. Do it in a maintenance window or low-risk time for anything stateful, keep a state backup before starting, and do it incrementally (one resource group at a time) rather than moving everything at once, so a mistake is easy to isolate and reverse.
Why do outputs and variable mappings nee: Once a resource moves inside a module, anything that referenced its output directly (e.g. `google_compute_instance.web.id`) must now go through the module's own output (`module.web.instance_id`), since the module boundary changes how that value is addressed - forgetting to update these references causes the configuration to fail to reference the resource that just moved.
What happens if a resource is removed fr: On the next `terraform apply`, Terraform sees the resource still exists in state but no longer in configuration, and plans to destroy it - the real infrastructure gets deleted. This is a common accidental-deletion trap when refactoring: removing a resource block without first doing a state move (if it was meant to just relocate, not delete) results in real infrastructure being destroyed.

Terraform loses all awareness of that resource - it won't plan to destroy it (since it's not in state) and the real infrastructure object keeps existing untouched in the cloud, now completely unmanaged by Terraform. This is the correct approach when you deliberately want Terraform to 'forget' a resource without deleting it (`terraform state rm` followed by removing the code block).
How would you optimize a Terraform pipel: Split state so a DNS-only change doesn't require Terraform to refresh/plan against the entire infrastructure's state (a smaller, scoped state file plans much faster), use `-target` sparingly for genuinely urgent one-off changes, and check whether the actual slowness is the provider's API (DNS providers can have slow propagation/API latency) versus Terraform's own plan/refresh time - if it's the provider, that's an inherent constraint of the DNS system itself, not something Terraform tuning can fix.
Explain every line of the for_each map c: `for r in var.records` iterates over each object in the input list; `"${r.name}-${r.type}"` builds a unique string key for that iteration by string-interpolating the record's name and type fields; `=> r` maps that key to the full original record object as the value, so the whole thing evaluates to a map Terraform can pass directly into `for_each` on the resource.
Explain how the DNS records are stored i: Each record is stored as a separate resource instance keyed by its for_each string (e.g. `aws_route53_record.records["www-A"]`), with the state entry holding both the attributes you specified (name, type, records) and everything AWS returned after creation (the record's fqdn, etc.) - this per-key storage is what lets Terraform add or remove one specific record on a future apply without touching any of the others.
The key is the unique string (`name-type` in this case) that identifies each map entry and becomes that resource instance's stable address suffix in state - it must be unique across all entries, known at plan time (not computed from a resource that doesn't exist yet), and stable across applies, since changing a key causes Terraform to see it as destroying the old instance and creating a new one rather than updating in place.
Fill the missing vpc_id reference in the:
vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
Reference the VPC resource's `id` attribute directly by its Terraform resource address rather than hardcoding a VPC ID string - this creates an implicit dependency so Terraform creates the VPC before anything referencing it, and automatically updates the reference if the VPC is ever recreated.
Complete main.tf using the given variabl: Wire each declared `variable` into the corresponding resource argument via `var.<name>` (e.g. `instance_type = var.instance_type`, `tags = var.tags`), and ensure any variable without a sensible default either has one set or is explicitly required via a `.tfvars` file - a variable declared but never referenced anywhere in a resource block is a strong signal something was left incomplete in the configuration.
A Layer 4 load balancer operates at the transport layer (TCP/UDP), routing based on IP and port without inspecting application content - fast and protocol-agnostic, but can't make routing decisions based on HTTP headers or paths. A Layer 7 load balancer operates at the application layer, understanding HTTP/HTTPS and able to route based on host, path, headers, or cookies (e.g. routing /api to one backend and /static to another), at the cost of slightly more processing overhead.
Which load balancer supports SSL termina: Both can, but it's most commonly done at Layer 7 (an Application Load Balancer) since terminating TLS there lets the load balancer inspect the decrypted HTTP request to make content-based routing decisions; a Network Load Balancer (Layer 4) can also do TLS termination in passthrough or termination mode but doesn't use the decrypted content for routing since it doesn't parse HTTP at all.
What backends can be attached to a Layer: EC2 instances, Auto Scaling Groups, IP addresses (including on-premises via VPN/Direct Connect), Lambda functions, and containers via ECS/EKS target groups - Application Load Balancers support routing to any of these as long as they're registered in a target group with a defined health check.
What is an SSL certificate?: A digitally signed file that binds a public key to an identity (a domain name), issued by a trusted Certificate Authority, that lets a client verify it's actually talking to the legitimate server (not an impersonator) and establish an encrypted TLS connection using the certificate's public/private key pair.
How do you obtain an SSL certificate?: Request one from a Certificate Authority - for AWS-hosted services, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues and auto-renews free public certificates validated via DNS or email; for other cases, a CA like Let's Encrypt (free, automatable via ACME protocol/certbot) or a commercial CA, typically by generating a CSR (Certificate Signing Request) with your domain and public key and completing domain-ownership validation.
What information is required to obtain a: The domain name(s) to be covered (including any wildcard/SAN entries needed), a public/private key pair (or letting the CA/ACM generate one), and proof of domain ownership - either a DNS validation record you add, or an email confirmation to an admin address on the domain, depending on the CA's validation method.
Web tier: an Application Load Balancer in public subnets fronting an Auto Scaling Group of web servers. Application tier: a second internal ALB or service discovery routing to an Auto Scaling Group of app servers in private subnets, with no direct internet access. Data tier: RDS (Multi-AZ for HA) in private subnets with security groups only allowing traffic from the app tier. Each tier sits in its own subnet with security groups scoped to only the traffic that tier actually needs from the tier above it.
Explain Route53 Resolver Inbound Endpoin: An Inbound Endpoint lets DNS queries originating outside AWS (from your on-premises network, over VPN/Direct Connect) resolve names hosted in Route53 private hosted zones - it's the entry point for external DNS resolvers to query into your VPC's private DNS namespace.
Explain Route53 Resolver Outbound Endpoi: An Outbound Endpoint lets DNS queries originating from within your VPC be forwarded out to DNS servers outside AWS (e.g. an on-premises DNS server), via conditional forwarding rules - used when resources in your VPC need to resolve names that only your on-prem DNS knows about, completing the hybrid DNS resolution path alongside the Inbound Endpoint.
Two VPCs need communication. How will yo: For simple, non-transitive connectivity between a small number of VPCs, VPC Peering (with route table entries and security group rules on both sides) is the straightforward option. For many VPCs needing to communicate (hub-and-spoke or full mesh), AWS Transit Gateway scales much better since it avoids the N-squared peering connections and non-transitivity limitations peering has.
What are the limitations of VPC Peering?: No transitive routing (if A is peered with B, and B with C, A cannot reach C through B - a direct A-C peering would be needed), no overlapping CIDR ranges between peered VPCs, a hard limit on the number of peering connections per VPC, and each connection must be individually managed (route tables, security groups) - which is why Transit Gateway is preferred once you're connecting more than a handful of VPCs.
Suppose an Auto Scaling Group has 10 ins: Check the target group's health check status first - if instances show unhealthy, the issue is likely the health check path/port misconfigured or the app itself not responding on it. If instances show healthy but the app is still inaccessible, check security groups (does the ALB's security group allow outbound to the instances, and do instances allow inbound from the ALB's security group specifically), then check the ALB's own listener rules and DNS/certificate configuration for the entry point itself.
What does \"Connection Reset by Peer\" m: The remote side (the peer) abruptly closed the TCP connection, typically by sending a RST packet, rather than gracefully closing it - common causes include the server-side process crashing or being killed mid-request, a load balancer/proxy timeout closing an idle connection the client thought was still open, or a security device/firewall actively terminating the connection.
If the application is healthy, what else: A load balancer or intermediate proxy's idle timeout being shorter than the client's own keep-alive expectation (the LB resets a connection the client assumed was still open), a security group or NACL change severing an established connection mid-session, server-side connection limits being hit and the OS resetting new/excess connections, or a client-side issue like sending data after the server already decided to close the connection.
Multiple RDS instances have multiple Sec: Iterate across the affected security groups and apply the same rule with the AWS CLI: `for sg in sg-aaa sg-bbb sg-ccc; do aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $sg --protocol tcp --port 5432 --cidr 10.0.0.0/16; done` - or, better for repeatability, express this as Terraform (a `for_each` over the list of security group IDs) so the change is version-controlled and idempotent rather than a one-off CLI loop.
Those resources are not managed by Terra: First bring them under Terraform management via `terraform import` for each existing security group (matched against a resource block you write describing its current configuration), then make the rule change through Terraform going forward so it's version-controlled and repeatable - directly scripting changes via CLI/SDK against unmanaged resources works as a one-off but doesn't prevent future drift or give you a change history.
How would you discover all the required: Use `aws rds describe-db-instances` (optionally filtered by tag, e.g. an environment or team tag) to enumerate all instances and their associated security groups programmatically, rather than manually clicking through the console - this also gives you a scriptable list to feed into the security-group-update loop or Terraform import commands.
Can Terraform deploy resources to Kubern: Yes - the Kubernetes provider lets Terraform manage Kubernetes objects (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, etc.) directly as Terraform resources, and the Helm provider lets Terraform install/manage Helm releases. This is common when Kubernetes resources are provisioned as part of the same Terraform run that creates the cluster itself, keeping infra and initial workload setup in one pipeline.
How does Terraform communicate with Kube: The Kubernetes provider authenticates to the cluster's API server (using a kubeconfig, a service account token, or cloud-specific auth like GKE's exec-based auth plugin) and issues standard Kubernetes API calls (the same API kubectl uses) to create/update/delete the resources declared in Terraform configuration.
Can Terraform manage Helm charts?: Yes, via the `helm_release` resource in the Helm provider - it lets Terraform install, upgrade, and manage the lifecycle of a Helm chart release declaratively as part of the same Terraform state as everything else, though many teams prefer keeping Helm/app deployments in a separate GitOps flow (ArgoCD/Flux) rather than mixing infrastructure and application deployment lifecycles in one Terraform state.
Can Terraform manage Datadog configurati: Yes - the Datadog provider manages monitors, dashboards, synthetic tests, and notification rules as Terraform resources, letting observability configuration be version-controlled and code-reviewed the same way infrastructure is, instead of being manually clicked together in the Datadog UI.
Can Terraform configure alerts?: Yes, via the `datadog_monitor` resource (or equivalent for other observability providers) - the alert condition (a metric query and threshold), notification message, and routing (which team/channel gets notified) are all defined as code, so alert changes go through the same PR review and history as any other infrastructure change.
Can Terraform configure dashboards?: Yes, via the `datadog_dashboard` resource, defining widgets and layout as Terraform configuration (often generated from a JSON dashboard export rather than hand-written, since dashboard JSON can be verbose) - this keeps dashboards reproducible across environments and prevents dashboard drift from undocumented manual UI edits.
How does Terraform authenticate to Datad: Via API and application key pair, typically supplied as provider configuration through environment variables (`DD_API_KEY`, `DD_APP_KEY`) rather than hardcoded in the provider block, so the actual credential values stay out of version control.
How are Datadog API credentials passed d: Stored as encrypted secrets in the CI/CD platform's secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, Jenkins Credentials) and injected as environment variables into the pipeline job at runtime, never checked into the repository - the same pattern used for any other cloud provider credential Terraform needs during apply.
What is RAID?: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple physical disks into one logical unit to improve performance, redundancy, or both, depending on the RAID level chosen - the tradeoff between usable capacity, fault tolerance, and speed differs significantly across levels.
RAID 0 stripes data across two or more disks with no redundancy - reads/writes are spread across disks for higher throughput, but a single disk failure loses all data on the array, since there's no parity or mirroring to reconstruct from. Used only where performance matters more than data safety (e.g. a scratch/cache volume with data reproducible elsewhere).
RAID 1 mirrors data identically across two (or more) disks - every write goes to all disks in the mirror, so any one disk can fail with zero data loss, at the cost of only getting the usable capacity of a single disk (50% efficiency for a 2-disk mirror) since the rest is pure duplication.
RAID 5 stripes data across at least three disks with distributed parity (parity blocks spread across all disks rather than one dedicated parity disk), tolerating a single disk failure while using only one disk's worth of capacity for parity overall - a good balance of capacity efficiency and fault tolerance for many workloads, though rebuild time after a failure can be slow on large disks.
RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping - disks are mirrored in pairs (RAID 1) and then those mirrored pairs are striped together (RAID 0), giving both the fault tolerance of mirroring (can survive multiple disk failures, as long as not both disks in the same mirrored pair fail) and the performance of striping, at the cost of 50% usable capacity, making it a common choice for performance- and reliability-sensitive database workloads.
What does mounting a filesystem mean?: Mounting attaches a filesystem (from a disk partition, network share, or other block device) to a specific directory (the mount point) in the existing directory tree, making its contents accessible through that path - before mounting, the filesystem's data exists on the device but isn't reachable through the normal filesystem hierarchy.
Which commands are used to mount a files: `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data` mounts a device at a mount point; `umount /mnt/data` unmounts it; `lsblk` and `blkid` help identify available devices and their filesystem types/UUIDs beforehand; `df -h` and `mount` (with no arguments) show currently mounted filesystems.
What happens after reboot if you only us: The mount is temporary - it only exists for the current running session, and after a reboot the filesystem is no longer mounted at that path, since `mount` alone doesn't persist configuration anywhere the boot process reads from.
How do you make a filesystem mount perma: Add an entry to `/etc/fstab` specifying the device (preferably by UUID rather than device name, since device names like /dev/sdb1 can shift across reboots), mount point, filesystem type, and mount options - the system reads this file at boot and mounts everything listed automatically, and `mount -a` can be used to test the fstab entry without rebooting.
How do you troubleshoot a crashed Linux: Check the serial/console output first if SSH is unreachable (often reveals a kernel panic or OOM killer log at the point of crash), check `journalctl -b -1` (logs from the previous boot) after it comes back up for what happened right before the crash, and check for hardware-level signals (disk errors in dmesg, a hypervisor/cloud console event) if it looks like an infrastructure-level rather than OS-level failure.
How do you check whether a port is open: `nc -zv <host> <port>` (netcat's zero-I/O scan mode) or `telnet <host> <port>` for a quick manual check; `nmap -p <port> <host>` for a more thorough scan including firewall behavior. This tests reachability from the client's perspective - a closed/filtered result distinguishes 'nothing listening' from 'a firewall is blocking it' based on the specific response (RST vs no response at all).
How do you measure network bandwidth bet: `iperf3` is the standard tool - run it in server mode on one host (`iperf3 -s`) and client mode on the other (`iperf3 -c <server-ip>`) to measure actual achievable throughput between them, which is far more reliable than inferring bandwidth from a single file transfer's speed (which is also affected by disk I/O, not just network).
How does Terraform authenticate with clo: Through provider-specific credential mechanisms configured outside the Terraform code itself where possible - for GCP, Application Default Credentials or a service account key/Workload Identity; for AWS, the standard credential chain (environment variables, shared credentials file, an IAM role attached to the execution environment). Best practice is never hardcoding credentials in the provider block, relying instead on environment-based or workload-identity-based auth so credentials aren't committed to version control.
How does Terraform communicate with prov: Terraform core launches each configured provider as a separate child process and communicates with it over a local gRPC connection using Terraform's internal plugin protocol - core sends generic operations (validate, plan, apply for a given resource type) and the provider translates them into actual API calls to the target platform, returning results back over the same protocol.
Explain the Terraform workflow (init, pl: `terraform init` downloads required providers/modules and sets up the backend for state. `terraform plan` computes the difference between current state and desired configuration, showing exactly what would be created/changed/destroyed without making any changes. `terraform apply` executes that plan (or a fresh one if none is passed) against the real infrastructure, updating state to reflect the new reality afterward.
Design a three-tier application with 3 w: A Load Balancer in a public subnet distributes traffic across the 3 web servers (also public-facing or in a DMZ subnet); web servers forward application requests to the 2 app servers in a private subnet (potentially behind an internal load balancer for their own redundancy); app servers connect to the database (in the most restricted private subnet, security group only allowing traffic from the app tier). Each tier's security group only permits inbound traffic from the tier directly above it, minimizing lateral attack surface.
Code is deployed tier by tier, typically app tier first then web tier (so new app-tier APIs exist before web tier code that calls them goes live), using a rolling or blue-green strategy per tier so there's always capacity serving traffic during the deploy. Health checks at the load balancer gate whether newly deployed instances receive traffic, and a deploy that fails health checks should automatically halt/rollback rather than proceeding to replace all instances.
A request enters through the Load Balancer (public), which forwards to a web server; the web server calls the application tier over the internal network (private subnet, not internet-routable); the app server queries the database over another private-subnet connection - at every hop, security groups restrict traffic to only the specific source tier and port needed, so a compromised web server, for example, still can't directly reach the database.
Each tier gets its own security group scoped to least privilege: the Load Balancer's security group allows inbound 443/80 from the internet; the web tier's security group allows inbound only from the Load Balancer's security group (referenced by security group ID, not IP range) on the app port; the app tier's allows inbound only from the web tier's security group; the database's allows inbound only from the app tier's security group on the DB port - chaining trust by security group reference rather than broad CIDR ranges.
Code merge triggers build and test, then a containerize/package step, then deployment to each tier in dependency order (database migrations first if needed, then app tier, then web tier) using the environment's standard rollout strategy (rolling/canary), with automated health checks gating progression between tiers and an automatic rollback path if any tier's health checks fail post-deploy.
